title: What are the Hibernate flush modes (AUTO, COMMIT, MANUAL/ALWAYS)? How do they control when pending changes are visible to a query?
shortTitle: Hibernate flush modes (AUTO, COMMIT, MANUAL) — when pending changes become visible to a query
topicTitle: What are the Hibernate flush modes

s1_definition.profdef: The flush mode controls *when* Hibernate automatically drains buffered changes to the database. `AUTO` (the default) flushes before the transaction commits **and** before executing a query whose results could be affected by pending changes, so queries stay consistent with in-memory state. `COMMIT` flushes only at commit, so a query may run against stale database state and miss un-flushed changes. `MANUAL` (JPA) / `NEVER` (legacy Hibernate) flushes **only** when you explicitly call `flush()`, giving you full control. Hibernate also has `ALWAYS`, which flushes before every query unconditionally.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the persistence context as a teller's working tray of unprocessed slips. AUTO means: before answering any customer question that could depend on those slips, and before closing the counter, the teller keys them all in first — so answers are always current. COMMIT means the teller only keys slips in at counter-close, so if a customer asks a balance mid-day it might ignore slips still in the tray. MANUAL means the teller keys slips in only when the manager explicitly says "process the tray now."
s1_definition.oneliner: AUTO flushes before affected queries and before commit (consistent); COMMIT flushes only at commit (queries can miss pending changes); MANUAL flushes only when you call flush().
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The flush mode controls *when* Hibernate automatically drains buffered changes to the database. `AUTO` (the default) flushes before the transaction commits **and** before executing a query whose results could be affected by pending changes, so queries stay consistent with in-memory state. `COMMIT` flushes only at commit, so a query may run against stale database state and miss un-flushed changes. `MANUAL` (JPA) / `NEVER` (legacy Hibernate) flushes **only** when you explicitly call `flush()`, giving you full control. Hibernate also has `ALWAYS`, which flushes before every query unconditionally.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the persistence context as a teller's working tray of unprocessed slips. AUTO means: before answering any customer question that could depend on those slips, and before closing the counter, the teller keys them all in first — so answers are always current. COMMIT means the teller only keys slips in at counter-close, so if a customer asks a balance mid-day it might ignore slips still in the tray. MANUAL means the teller keys slips in only when the manager explicitly says "process the tray now."

**One line to remember:** AUTO flushes before affected queries and before commit (consistent); COMMIT flushes only at commit (queries can miss pending changes); MANUAL flushes only when you call flush().

sections.s2_technical:
The flush mode is set on the session or per query, and it answers one question: before this query runs, should Hibernate push pending changes to the database so the query sees them?

With **AUTO**, the default, Hibernate is smart. Before running a query it checks whether the query touches tables that have pending inserts, updates, or deletes in the action queue; if so, it flushes first so the query returns correct, up-to-date results. It also always flushes before commit. This is why, inside a transaction, if you change an account's balance and then run a JPQL query filtering on balance, the query reflects your change.

```java
account.setBalance(new BigDecimal("0"));  // pending change
// AUTO flushes before this query because it touches the accounts table
List<Account> empty = em.createQuery(
    "select a from Account a where a.balance = 0", Account.class).getResultList();
```

With **COMMIT**, Hibernate only flushes at commit time, not before queries. So in the example above, the query might run before the balance change is flushed and would miss it, returning potentially stale data. You set it when you deliberately do not want query-triggered flushes, often for performance in read-heavy flows, accepting the tradeoff.

```java
em.setFlushMode(FlushModeType.COMMIT);  // JPA
// or per query:
query.setFlushMode(FlushModeType.COMMIT);
```

With **MANUAL** (JPA `FlushModeType` does not include MANUAL directly; Hibernate exposes `FlushMode.MANUAL`), nothing flushes automatically — not even before commit in the Hibernate-native sense — until you call `session.flush()`. This is used in advanced multi-step conversations where you build up changes across several requests and flush only at a controlled point.

Senior nuances: native SQL queries do not participate in AUTO's table-dirtiness detection reliably, so Hibernate may flush everything before a native query to be safe, or you may need an explicit flush. Choosing COMMIT can cause subtle bugs where a query does not see your own pending write, so use it only when you understand the read semantics. And MANUAL demands discipline — forgetting to flush means changes silently never reach the database.
sections.s3_banking:
**Problem 1 — a report query inside a transaction must reflect a just-made adjustment.** At National Bank of India, a correction updates an account's balance, then a summary query must include that corrected figure. With AUTO this just works because Hibernate flushes before the query. This is exactly what AUTO guarantees.

**Problem 2 — a read-heavy screen was flushing on every lookup and slowing down.** A dashboard ran many queries in one transaction while holding minor pending changes, and AUTO kept flushing before each query. Switching that read path to COMMIT flush mode removed the extra flushes. This is exactly the AUTO-versus-COMMIT tradeoff.

What the code will do: an `AdjustmentService` showing AUTO making a pending change visible to a query, and a `DashboardService` using COMMIT mode on a read-heavy query path.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: zero out SAV2001's balance, then count accounts with balance zero.

Step 1 — SAV2001 is loaded as managed; its snapshot records balance 1000000.

Step 2 — `setBalance(ZERO)` changes the in-memory balance; nothing is flushed yet, so the database still shows 1000000.

Step 3 — the JPQL query runs with AUTO. Hibernate sees the query touches the accounts table and there is a pending change on an Account, so it flushes first, writing balance zero to the database within the transaction.

Step 4 — the query now runs against the flushed state and returns SAV2001, so the count includes it. With COMMIT mode the flush would have been skipped and the query would have missed the pending change.

Step 5 — in the dashboard path, COMMIT mode runs several balance queries without a pre-query flush each time, reducing overhead; the read-only transaction commits with nothing to write.

```
2026-10-24 01:15:02 INFO  AUTO: query sees the pending zero balance → count = 1
2026-10-24 01:15:03 INFO  COMMIT mode: 2 queries ran without pre-query flushes
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Flush Modes (FAANG Level) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Strategy-like policy: flush mode per session/query        │
  │  Unit of Work: context decides when to drain               │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: each service owns one read/write concern               │
  │  O: tune flush mode per query without changing entities    │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Decision Table (as prose) ──
  AUTO   : flush before affected query + before commit → consistent (default)
  COMMIT : flush only at commit → queries may miss pending writes → faster reads
  MANUAL : flush only on explicit flush() → full control, needs discipline
  ALWAYS : flush before every query unconditionally → safest, slowest

  ── State Diagram: pending change visibility ──
  [pending in context]
     │ AUTO + affected query → flush → [visible to query]
     │ COMMIT → [NOT visible until commit]
     │ MANUAL → visible only after explicit flush()

  ── Call Chain (AUTO) ──
  1. find → MANAGED  2. setBalance(0) pending
  3. query balance=0 → AUTO detects dirty table → flush
  4. query returns zeroed row → 5. commit

  ⚠ COMMIT can hide your own write from your own query.
  ⚠ MANUAL: forgetting flush() silently drops changes.
  Rule: default AUTO; COMMIT for read-heavy; MANUAL for controlled conversations.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The flush mode controls when Hibernate automatically drains the persistence context to the database. The default, auto, flushes before the transaction commits and, crucially, before running a query whose results could be affected by pending changes, so inside a transaction my queries always stay consistent with my in-memory writes. Commit mode flushes only at commit, so a query may run against stale database state and miss changes I have made but not yet flushed. Manual mode flushes only when I explicitly call flush, which gives me complete control at the cost of having to remember to do it, and there is also an always mode that flushes before every query unconditionally.

The reason auto is the safe default is that Hibernate inspects each query, and if it touches a table that has pending inserts, updates, or deletes in the action queue, it flushes first so the query returns correct results. That is why if I zero an account's balance and then run a query filtering on balance equal to zero, the query includes that account even though I never explicitly flushed. Commit mode trades that guarantee for fewer flushes, which helps a read-heavy path that holds minor pending changes and runs many queries, but it can introduce subtle bugs where a query does not see my own pending write, so I use it only where I understand the read semantics.

At National Bank of India I used auto on our correction path, where an adjustment updates a balance and a summary query must include the corrected figure, and it simply worked because Hibernate flushed before the query. On a dashboard that ran many balance lookups in one transaction, auto was flushing before every read and slowing things down, so I switched that read-only path to commit flush mode and removed the extra flushes. The nuances I always mention are that native SQL queries do not reliably participate in auto's table-dirtiness detection, so Hibernate may flush everything before a native query to be safe, and that manual mode demands discipline because a forgotten flush means the changes silently never reach the database.
